title: Why Do Traffic Jams Appear From Nowhere? #traffic
description:
A jam with no cause is a wave: each driver reacts a little late and brakes a little harder, and the slowdown travels backwards through the cars at about 20 km/h.

Full video: Why do traffic jams appear out of nowhere? → https://youtu.be/Rwx3Y7Pw9rk

Sources
- Sugiyama et al. (2008), Traffic jams without bottlenecks, New Journal of Physics 10, 033001
- Bando et al. (1995), Dynamical model of traffic congestion, Physical Review E 51, 1035
- Stern et al. (2018), Dissipation of stop-and-go waves via control of autonomous vehicles, Transportation Research Part C 89
- Green (2000), How long does it take to stop?, Transportation Human Factors 2(3)

subtitles: Why do traffic jams appear from nowhere?
In a 2008 study in Japan, 22 cars drove around a ring, 230 metres long.
The road was crowded but clear.
Within minutes, a jam appeared anyway.
The next reacts late, and brakes a little harder.
Each car passes it back, bigger, until cars almost stop.
So a jam is a wave.
Cars move forward, but the jam slides backwards, at about 20 km/h.
That's why you crawl through a jam, and find nothing there.
